Remedies for Breach of Contract 
201
Taking into account the situation of the debtor and the needs of the creditor, a 
court may defer payment of sums that are due, or allow it to be made in instal­
ments, for a period no greater than two years.
By a special, reasoned decision, a court may order that sums corresponding to 
deferred instalments shall bear interest at a reduced rate (not lower than the legal 
rate of interest) or that any payments made will first be allocated to repayment of 
capital.
The court may make these measures subject to the debtor effecting acts appro­
priate to facilitate or to secure payment of the debt.
A délai de grâce usually takes the form of an order allowing deferred payment or 
payment in instalments.34 Its effect is to postpone the right of the injured party to 
enforce the debt, allowing more time for the defaulting party to raise the amount 
owing.35 Performance is therefore delayed, not excused.36 This is justified on 
grounds of fairness37 and beneficence to the defaulting party who is unable to fulfil 
a payment obligation despite acting in good faith.38 It also serves to promote the 
performance of the contract, with late performance thought to be preferable to no 
performance at all.39
The potential for a délai de grâce to prejudice the interests of the injured party 
is limited by a requirement that the court, when exercising the discretion, balance 
their needs with those of the defaulting party. It is also open to the court to require 
the defaulting party to take steps to facilitate or guarantee the payment of the debt.
(c)  The specific enforcement of non-​monetary obligations
French courts similarly show little hesitation in granting the specific enforcement
of non-​monetary obligations. It is a remedy that is available to the injured party as
of right40 and extremely broad in scope.41 The defaulting party can be compelled to 
perform in a wide array of circumstances.
